introduction: “The best beloved of all things in My sight is Justice … By its aid thou shalt see with thine own eyes and not through the eyes of others.” In this Hidden Word Bahá’u’lláh ties two things that are usually treated apart: justice toward others and independence of mind. The word He uses most often beside ‘adl, justice, is inṣáf: fairness, giving each thing its due, and it applies first to how one looks. A fair-minded person examines a claim with his own eyes, holds his own beliefs to the test he applies to others’, and does not let desire or prejudice decide. From there the readings move to dealings with others, to the conduct of those in authority, and to the statement that “the first quality of human nature is fairness.” The outside quotations follow the same path: the Bereans and Nicodemus on hearing before judging; Proverbs, Mill and Bacon on weighing both sides; the Law and the prophets on judging without respect of persons; the Qur’án’s “staunch in justice … even though it be against yourselves”; Augustine and Pascal on justice in the state. Hume asks whether reason can ever be anything but the servant of desire, and Shylock asks for the fairness he has been refused.
questions: “By its aid thou shalt see with thine own eyes.” Why should justice be the faculty that makes independent seeing possible?
“Beware lest desire deprive you of equity.” Recall a judgment you made that suited your interest. How would you test it now?
“Even though it be against yourselves or your parents or your kindred.” When did fairness last cost you something?
“The world is in need of two things: order and justice.” What happens, in Augustine’s and Pascal’s account and in your experience, when a society has one without the other?
The last reading applies fairness to the treatment of women. Where else does the test “as they do not allow … upon themselves” still wait to be applied?

outside.why: By the aid of justice “thou shalt see with thine own eyes and not through the eyes of others.” Jesus: judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment.
To “know of thine own knowledge.” Paul: prove all things; hold fast that which is good.

That they “may see with their own eyes and hear with their own ears.” Luke calls the Bereans noble for it: they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
“The first quality of human nature is fairness, and all matters depend upon it.” Aristotle: this form of justice is complete virtue, and is often thought to be the greatest of virtues.
“Beware lest desire deprive you of equity.” Jeremiah: the heart is deceitful above all things: who can know it?

Hume doubted that the mind is ever free of desire’s direction: reason is, and ought only to be the slave of the passions. If he is right, is fair-mindedness possible? What do the readings count on to make it so?
To speak with fairness, “not according to the promptings of his desires.” Proverbs: the way of a fool is right in his own eyes: but he that hearkeneth unto counsel is wise.
“By what proof and evidence did ye acknowledge the Bayán?” Hold the new claim to the same test. Proverbs: he that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him.
The same measure for one’s own beliefs as for another’s. Jesus: why beholdest thou the mote that is in thy brother’s eye, but considerest not the beam that is in thine own eye?
Fairness as a wine that “may open an eye.” Nicodemus asked his colleagues for no more than that: doth our law judge any man, before it hear him, and know what he doeth?
That they may “recognize this Day and what hath appeared therein.” Gamaliel’s fairness to a new movement: if this work be of men, it will come to nought: but if it be of God, ye cannot overthrow it.
“Deal with them in fairness and justice.” Jesus: all things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them.
“Deal with one another with the utmost justice and equity.” The Qur’án: be ye staunch in justice, witnesses for Allah, even though it be against yourselves or your parents or your kindred.

“Thou hast not been in Our company, thou art therefore ignorant of the Cause … scrutinize the Writings with thine own eyes.” Proverbs: he that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him.
Mill: he who knows only his own side of the case, knows little of that.
“In this sharing be praiseworthy and just.” Leviticus: thou shalt not respect the person of the poor, nor honour the person of the mighty: but in righteousness shalt thou judge thy neighbour.
“Practice justice towards all men.” The Qur’án extends it to enemies: let not hatred of any people seduce you that ye deal not justly.
True honour: “exercise justice and equity … and work for the good of his fellow-citizens.” Micah: to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God.
The fair-minded “are the trustees of the earth and its people.” The psalm’s charge to those in trust: do justice to the afflicted and needy.
“The world is in need of two things: order and justice.” Augustine on order without justice: justice being taken away, then, what are kingdoms but great robberies?
Pascal on why both are needed: justice without might is helpless; might without justice is tyrannical.
“Justice hath ever been and shall ever be beloved.” Proverbs: to do justice and judgment is more acceptable to the Lord than sacrifice.
Blessed is he who has “cast oppression behind him, holding fast to fairness.” Isaiah: cease to do evil; learn to do well; seek judgment, relieve the oppressed.
A hope that “the edifice of oppression will fall.” Amos: let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream.

A prayer that a governor may act “with justice and fairness.” Solomon’s own prayer on taking office: give therefore thy servant an understanding heart to judge thy people, that I may discern between good and bad.
“Dawning-places of justice and equity … unto all who are on earth.” Moses to the judges: ye shall hear the small as well as the great; ye shall not be afraid of the face of man.
Commanded to justice night and day, “yet most have preferred passion.” Isaiah: judgment is turned away backward; for truth is fallen in the street, and equity cannot enter.
To “behold with thine own eyes.” Bacon’s rule for a reader: read not to contradict and confute; nor to believe and take for granted; but to weigh and consider.
Justice is “for man to free himself from idle fancy and imitation … and look into all things with a searching eye.” Socrates: the life which is unexamined is not worth living.
As men do not allow oppression of themselves, “they must not allow it upon the handmaidens.” Job on those in his household: did not he that made me in the womb make him?

Shylock demands the same imagination from those who despise him: hath not a Jew eyes? hath not a Jew hands, organs, dimensions, senses, affections, passions? Whom do you find it hardest to see as you see yourself, and what would fairness to them require?
